parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis: the model adds a linear score over the inputs (the direct terms) and a set of small corrections from the hidden parts on the logit scale, and a sigmoid turns the sum into the predicted probability of the lower income class of the census income data. No part feeds another, so the corrections add on the score. Prediction: changing one input moves just the parts that read it and leaves the rest where they were. Self-probe: sweeping capital gain on the typical case from 0 US dollars to 99999 US dollars leaves the education part at 0.376 and 0.376 and the husband gate at 0.737 and 0.737, while the capital-gain part moves from 0.09 to -58.9, as predicted. On the typical training case (age 37 years, a married husband and high-school graduate in a private-sector professional job) the predicted lower-income probability is 70%. Switching all the hidden parts off together lowers training AUC from 0.9064 to 0.8873; replacing the direct terms by their mean lowers it to 0.6458, so the linear score carries most of the ranking. By AUC loss when switched off alone, the largest hidden parts are education (to 0.8959), capital gain (to 0.9031) and the husband gate (to 0.9047). The annotated model reproduces the original network's output on every training row to within 6.7e-16.

parts.original_hypothesis: The direct edges form a linear score over the z-scored inputs (the formula is attached as evidence). Among the direct weights per sd are capital gain -1.99, married to a civilian spouse -1.75, own child 0.88, never worked 0.68, sex (male) -0.60, other-service occupation 0.54, age -0.51, hours per week -0.46, a birthplace in the outlying US territories 0.39 (on 20 training rows) and education-num -0.35; a negative weight lowers the predicted probability of the lower income class. One sizeable edge, for a birthplace in the Netherlands (-0.87 per sd), has 0 training rows behind it. Prediction: marriage and age move the score along straight lines with these signs. Self-probe on the typical case: changing marital status from married to never married moves this part from -2.56 to 0.91 and the predicted lower-income probability from 70% to 99%; age from 20 years to 70 years lowers this part in equal steps from -1.93 to -3.79 (whole model: 81% to 40%). Age feeds the direct edge alone (it has no edge into a hidden unit), so its whole-model effect is this straight line. Replacing the direct terms by their mean lowers training AUC from 0.9064 to 0.6458: the linear score carries most of the ranking.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient); an input the data ties to a category takes its typical value within that category (linked inputs)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording

summary.text: The model treats a higher capital gains as clearly lowering the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) slowly at first, then faster: for a typical person, it goes from about 70% at 0 US dollars to about 9% at 6849 US dollars, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted risk cannot go much lower.

For a typical person, the model gives a lower predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) if the highest education is doctorate (with education level (1 = preschool to 16 = doctorate) at 16 on the 1-16 scale, as in the data) (about 17%) than if highest education is something other than 10th grade, doctorate, master's degree, preschool, some college, 1st-4th grade, associate degree (academic) (about 70%) (on the training data only).

The model treats a higher education level as clearly lowering the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) in stages: for a typical person, it goes from about 80% at 7 on the 1-16 scale to about 30% at 13 on the 1-16 scale (with highest education at bachelor's degree, as in the data).

The model gives a clearly higher predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) if the country of birth is India than if country of birth is something other than India, and even more so if the person is a husband: for a typical person, going from country of birth other than India to India moves the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) from about 70% to about 95% if the person is a husband, and from about 97% to about 99% if relationship in the household is something other than husband (with marital status at never married, as in the data).

A higher education level clearly lowers the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less), and even more so if the country of birth is Germany (in stages for people whose country of birth is Germany): for a typical person, education level going from 7 on the 1-16 scale to 13 on the 1-16 scale moves the predicted chance of a low income ($50,000 or less) from about 77% to about 21% if the country of birth is Germany, and from about 80% to about 30% if country of birth is something other than Germany.
